title: Timers
learningObjectives: Explain timers and handle asynchronous browser work safely.

understand.concept: setTimeout schedules a callback after at least the requested delay; setInterval schedules repeated callbacks. Delays are not exact execution guarantees because the event loop, browser throttling, and page state affect when callbacks run. clearTimeout and clearInterval cancel scheduled timers.
understand.whyItMatters: Timers are useful for delays and periodic updates, but they should not be treated as precise clocks. Long-running intervals can overlap work or waste resources if not cleaned up.
understand.analogy: A timer is a reminder placed in a queue, not a promise that someone will interrupt the current task at an exact instant.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; JavaScript scheduling and browser security follow platform-defined rules.

explain.narrative: The one-time callback runs after a minimum delay; the interval is stopped after roughly 3.2 seconds. Actual timing may vary.

examples.explanation: The one-time callback runs after a minimum delay; the interval is stopped after roughly 3.2 seconds. Actual timing may vary.
examples.expectedOutput: Console or interface behaviour demonstrates the asynchronous concept; network examples require a suitable endpoint.

practise.guidedTask: Create a countdown using recursive setTimeout or setInterval. Cancel it when the countdown ends and explain why the delay is not exact.
practise.independentTask: Build a small asynchronous interface. Handle loading, success, empty, cancellation, and failure states where applicable.
hints: Do not assume a zero-delay timer runs immediately.
Check HTTP status separately from network failure.
Validate response data before rendering it.

questions.prompt: Which function cancels a timer created by setInterval()?
questions.explanation: clearInterval cancels a repeating interval using its returned identifier.

questions.prompt: What is a good rule for asynchronous UI code?
options: Represent loading, success, empty, and error states explicitly
Treat every completed HTTP response as success
questions.answer: Represent loading, success, empty, and error states explicitly
questions.explanation: Explicit states make asynchronous interfaces understandable and resilient.
